 Residents feeling the shock of record heating oil costs 
 LIHEAP assistance application process opens Nov. 2

 According to the US Energy Information Administration, heating oil prices are reaching an all-time high and a rise of approximately 85% from the same period last year. (GETTY)
 By Gregory Adams | gadams@standardspeaker.com | Standard Speaker PUBLISHED: October 30, 2026 at 11:34 AM EDT | UPDATED: October 30, 2026 at 11:41 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Sandy Dickison of Old Forge has had oil heat in her home for the past 20 years and would typically pay around $2.50 to $3.75 per gallon.
 Her last oil delivery was Sept. 18 and it cost $1,565 to fill her 275-gallon tank, at $5.69 per gallon.
 “We usually fill up our tank four times times a year,” Dickison said. “It also heats our water, so we need it year-round. That would be approximately 1,100 gallons. At the current rate, that is $6,259.”
 Dickison added she and her family have been cutting back on some luxuries such as shopping and going out to eat as the heating oil prices carve out more of their household budget than she would like.
 Heating oil prices have reached an all-time high, rising more than 85% from the same period last year, the U.S. Energy Information Administration reports. The average cost of a gallon of heating oil in late October 2026 is $6.05 compared to $3.24 in mid-October 2025, according to the agency. The surge is largely driven by supply disruptions linked to the war in Iran, according to industry sources and the The National Energy Assistance Directors Association.
 Prices have also eclipsed a spike in 2022 following the COVID-19 pandemic, when mid-October prices topped out around $5.75 per gallon.
 Dickison said she’s still purchasing her usual amount but is trying to conserve by turning off her furnace during the day and limiting her usage to nighttime.
 There is help for families struggling with high heating prices through the federally funded Low Income Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP).
 The application window to apply opens Nov. 2 and runs until May 8 for a one-time cash grant of $200 to $1,000.
 The grant does not have to be repaid and the amount families can receive is based on household size, income and fuel type.
 In addition to the regular grant, crisis grants are also offered through application for emergency relief for urgent situations such as a broken main heating source or a looming service shut-off .
 Although Dickison has already received her first shipment of heating oil for the year, her family is already in the process of switching to natural gas. She said the changeover can take up to three months to complete. If it isn’t completed by the dead of winter, she will just purchase minimal oil shipments until it is.
 “Our natural gas changeover is to help costs in the long run,” she said. “It will not help us this year and into half of next year due to the new furnace replacement costs. But, by next year’s heating season, we should start to see some savings.”
 To apply for a LIHEAP grant you can call the LIHEAP Hotline at 1-866-857-7095 or apply online through the state’s COMPASS Benefits site at www.compass.dhs.pa.gov.
